plate_findings.evidence: hypercellular marrow with increased megakaryocytes

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Bone marrow biopsy histology from a patient with refractory primary immune thrombocytopenia showing hypercellular marrow and increased megakaryocytes. B: Reticulin stain of bone marrow biopsy from ITP patient demonstrating myelofibrosis with increased reticulin fibers. C: Masson trichrome stain of bone marrow biopsy from ITP patient demonstrating collagen bundles and myelofibrosis.
panels.attribution_text: Kim et al. Romiplostim-related myelofibrosis in refractory primary immune thrombocytopenia: A Case report.. Medicine 2019. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000015882. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: A: Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow with increased megakaryocytes and myelofibrosis (H&E stain, ×100). B: A reticulin stain and C: Masson trichrome stain revealed an increase in diffuse and dense reticulin fibers with focal collagen bundles (MF-2) (×100).
in_text_mentions: eaction (Fig. 1); however, the bone marrow aspiration smear was inadequate for evaluation, and the bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hypercellular marrow, with 90% cellularity, proliferation of pleomorphic megakaryocytes, and myelofibrosis (Fig. 2A). A reticulin stain and Masson trichrome stain revealed an increase in diffuse and dense reticulin fibers, with focal bundles of collagen (MF-2) (Fig. 2B, C). The patient was diagnosed with romiplostim-induced myelofibrosis. Since this diagnosis, romiplostim was discontinued, and the patient received platelet apheresis transfusions every three months.

in_text_mentions: A 72-year-old male with hypertension, hepatitis C (treated), liver transplant in 2012 (off immunosuppressants), and recent colorectal surgery, presented from a skilled nursing facility with urinary retention and abdominal discomfort. One month earlier, he had undergone open low anterior resection for a rectosigmoid tubulovillous adenoma. His postoperative course was complicated by urinary retention, requiring Foley catheterization and discharge with the catheter in place (Figure 1).

Written informed consent for publication of clinical details and identifying images, including Figure 1A, was obtained from the patient, and a signed consent statement has been provided to the journal.

in_text_mentions: The patient had been in his usual state of health until he developed a rapidly progressive mixed purpuric/petechial rash on his upper extremities and oral bleeding (Figure 1). He presented to his primary care provider (PCP) who performed a CBC that revealed severe thrombocytopenia (2,000 platelets, reference >150,000). A CBC from only three months prior had been normal, and all his prior CBCs had been hitherto unremarkable. As a result, he was referred to our tertiary care center for further management.

His physical examination was notable for normal vital signs and remarkable for purpura on the bilateral upper extremities, a petechial rash on the bilateral lower extremities, and oral mucocutaneous lesions (not shown) (Figure 1). His neurologic and abdominal examinations were both unremarkable.
